chunks.section: EnergyCal: Taming Loss Spikes in Muon-Family Optimizers for Sparse MoE Training
chunks.text: Masato Fujitake

Sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) language-model training can exhibit large loss spikes with Muon-family optimizers. We introduce EnergyCal, a lightweight rule that attenuates routed-expert updates according to the normalized squared Frobenius norm of their finite-step Newton–Schulz directions. EnergyCal leaves the spectral transform unchanged and adds no persistent optimizer state. We evaluate it on a 4B-parameter MoE model. Against a development-selected, lower-learning-rate MuonH recipe, EnergyCal–MuonH reduces mean thresholded loss-spike burden by 99.51% and final geometric-mean perplexity by 4.06%, with a modest throughput cost. With plain Muon at matched nominal learning rate and weight decay, the reduction in mean spike burden averages 95.98% across the two tested exponents, accompanied by small endpoint improvements. These findings support stabilization both with and without Hyperball in the evaluated setting.

Sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models route tokens unevenly across experts, creating time-varying optimization conditions [ 1 ] . This setting can be challenging for Muon-family optimizers, which use Newton–Schulz (NS) iterations to transform momentum-based updates. Muon has shown promise for language-model pretraining [ 2 , 3 , 4 ] , while Hyperball introduces explicit control over weight and update norms [ 5 ] . Its Muon variant, MuonH, normalizes update directions and projects weights onto a fixed-radius sphere. In our custom 4B-parameter DeepSeekMoE-style model, both Muon and MuonH exhibit intermittent loss spikes, although all full-schedule runs complete. We investigate whether these loss excursions can be mitigated through a simple modification of routed-expert updates.

An expert can retain nonzero momentum even when no tokens are assigned to it in the current step. This motivates examining expert-wise update magnitudes, particularly under MuonH’s fixed-norm normalization. We propose EnergyCal, a lightweight rule that attenuates each routed-expert update according to the normalized squared Frobenius norm of its finite-step NS direction. Figure 1 illustrates the method. The coefficient is bounded between zero and one and is applied continuously during training. EnergyCal leaves the NS transform, momentum, and router objective unchanged, requires no token-utilization statistics, and adds no persistent optimizer state. Its energy statistic is not scale-invariant stable rank: low energy can reflect direction concentration, amplitude, or both. We evaluate EnergyCal in two separate full-schedule studies, each using three initialization seeds. First, a frozen EnergyCal–MuonH recipe reduces mean thresholded loss-spike burden by 99.51% and final geometric-mean perplexity by 4.06% relative to a development-selected, lower-learning-rate MuonH recipe, with 1.62% lower mean throughput. Second, applying EnergyCal to plain Muon at matched nominal learning rate and weight decay reduces mean spike burden by 95.98% on average across the two tested exponents, with small endpoint improvements. Together, these results show that stabilization is observed both with and without Hyperball in the evaluated MoE setting. However, plain Muon retains intermediate-quality and speed advantages in the first study, and different evaluation banks prevent a direct ranking of the calibrated optimizer families.

Our contribution is an empirical evaluation of one-sided, post-NS energy attenuation across MuonH and plain Muon. Unlike utilization- or alignment-guided expert scaling methods [ 6 , 7 ] , EnergyCal relies only on the energy of each logical matrix’s NS direction. The results do not establish general optimizer superiority or identify the cause of individual spikes: single-update interventions fail to rescue two examined events, and the plain-Muon study lacks a routed-only uniform-scaling control to separate energy-dependent attenuation from a simpler reduction in update magnitude. We therefore focus on the measured stability benefits and their practical trade-offs within the tested setting; Section 7 discusses these evidence boundaries.

Muon-family optimization and Hyperball. Muon applies a short Newton–Schulz (NS) iteration to momentum-based matrix updates [ 2 ] . Large-scale studies identify weight decay and update scaling as important for Muon pretraining [ 4 ] . Our plain-Muon baseline uses a shape factor of one rather than the full Moonlight recipe. Hyperball controls update and weight radii; its Muon variant, MuonH, normalizes trial directions and projects weights onto a fixed-radius sphere [ 5 ] . EnergyCal changes routed-expert step magnitudes after NS without changing the spectral transform. Expert-wise update scaling. Existing methods scale expert updates using other signals. Excitation uses expert utilization [ 6 ] , while ExpertMuon-Compass uses post-orthogonalization gradient alignment across experts and rows [ 7 ] . EnergyCal instead computes an independent coefficient q ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] q\in[0,1] from each routed matrix’s normalized squared post-NS Frobenius norm, without utilization inputs or cross-expert normalization. For q > 0 q>0 , scalar scaling preserves the NS direction; when q = 0 q=0 , the directional trial vanishes. Neither case guarantees the direction of the stored parameter displacement after Hyperball projection or low-precision writeback. Direction preservation itself is not unique to EnergyCal. Magnitude and spectral corrections. NorMuon uses neuron-level normalization after orthogonalization [ 8 ] , and TrasMuon uses RMS calibration and energy-based clipping [ 9 ] . Thus, energy-aware scaling is not new by itself. Pion changes NS iterations [ 10 ] , while SoftMuon uses smooth spectral relaxation [ 11 ] . EnergyCal instead applies a matrix-level scalar after the unchanged NS transform. We do not report native-method head-to-head comparisons with these alternatives.

Training stability in sparse models. Training instability in sparse MoE models has motivated router-centered approaches, including ST-MoE’s router z-loss and methods for reducing routing fluctuations [ 12 , 13 ] . Spike-aware optimization has also been studied in dense language-model training through momentum resets and gradient clipping [ 14 ] . Unlike these approaches, EnergyCal attenuates routed-expert updates using post-NS direction energy without modifying routing objectives or introducing spike-triggered interventions. Finite-step orthogonalization. Recent analyses characterize the convergence and spectral behavior of Muon with finite-step Newton–Schulz iterations [ 15 , 16 ] . MuonEq further investigates pre-NS equilibration to improve the geometry of orthogonalized updates [ 17 ] . EnergyCal instead leaves the NS transform unchanged and applies a matrix-level attenuation coefficient to its returned direction. Evaluation and optimizer comparisons. Optimizer rankings depend on tuning and training budget [ 18 ] ; angular effective learning rates also complicate the interpretation of Hyperball’s nominal learning rate [ 19 ] . We therefore report final quality, intermediate quality, loss-spike burden, and throughput separately. Matched nominal learning rate does not imply matched parameter movement, and fixed-token quality is distinct from equal-wall-time quality.

We train a custom 4B-parameter DeepSeekMoE-style language model from scratch, with 24 layers, hidden width 1,536, 128 routed experts of width 256 and top-2 routing, and one shared expert per layer. Its input and output embeddings are tied. The routed/shared design follows DeepSeekMoE [ 20 ] , with a separate traffic-driven router-bias controller [ 21 , 22 ] . Neither mechanism enters EnergyCal’s coefficient. Each run uses eight H100 80GB GPUs, 2,048-token sequences, and 131,072 tokens per optimizer update. A complete run has 10,000 updates (1.31B tokens), with 500 warmup updates followed by cosine decay to 10% of peak learning rate. All methods use gradient clipping at norm 1, five NS iterations, and the same logical matrix partitions. These experiments do not claim compute-optimal or fully converged pretraining. Appendix A gives the relevant implementation details. Training uses FineWeb sample-10BT [ 23 ] , with a deterministic train/validation partition. All final runs share the same data order; the independently varied initialization seeds do not constitute independently sampled corpora. Validation uses a fixed 524,288-token bank evaluated every 500 updates. Banks are fixed within each comparison but differ between development, Cohort H, and Cohort M. They are not certified previously unused external test sets across the complete exploratory history.

chunks.section: 5.2 Intermediate quality and the late crossover

The mean ordering reverses between the observed 8000- and 8500-step evaluations (supplementary Fig. 4 ). Thus, EnergyCal’s endpoint advantage emerges late in the schedule rather than persisting throughout training. Appendix B gives the run-level summaries and late-window comparison. chunks.section: 6.2 Single-update interventions do not rescue two events
chunks.text: Candidate-only EnergyCal reduces actual BF16-stored operator displacement by 86.3% (A) and 76.3% (B), while exact freezing eliminates that candidate displacement. Nevertheless, next-step CE remains near 6.3 and 6.9, respectively. In the common short windows, candidate freezing reduces burden by 3.09% and 0.76%, compared with 1.61% and 1.40% for control freezing. Applying EnergyCal to all routed matrices for a single update reduces short-window burden by 2.12% in event A but increases it by 3.41% in event B. This short-window burden is distinct from the full-schedule B 1 B_{1} defined in Eq. ( 12 ). A separate fixed-input 512-token probe shows no large reduction in output KL; probe CE decreases slightly in every branch. The probe differs from the next high-loss training batch and omits the subsequent router-bias update. These interventions therefore do not explain continuous calibration’s observed full-schedule benefit through immediate removal of the two examined spikes, but they do not establish that smaller or history-dependent effects are absent.

Empirical contribution and practical trade-offs. The main finding is a substantial reduction in thresholded loss-spike burden with both MuonH and plain Muon, accompanied by small improvements in final validation quality. In Cohort H, the frozen EnergyCal–MuonH recipe reduces mean burden by 99.51% relative to a development-selected, lower-rate MuonH recipe, with improved endpoint quality and 1.62% lower mean throughput. Because the learning rates differ, this comparison does not isolate the effect of calibration alone. The plain-Muon comparator is faster and achieves better intermediate quality; an illustrative equal-time estimate can also favor plain Muon. In Cohort M, EnergyCal reduces mean burden by 95.98% on average across two tested exponents at matched nominal learning rate and weight decay, showing that stabilization is also observed without Hyperball. However, different validation banks preclude a direct quality ranking of the calibrated optimizer families, and no production-style throughput benchmark is available for Cohort M. These results support empirical stabilization in the evaluated setting, not general optimizer superiority.

The unresolved uniform-scaling alternative. EnergyCal attenuates routed-expert updates, but the observed improvements need not arise specifically from assigning different coefficients according to direction energy. Cohort M lacks a routed-only uniform-scaling or update-budget-matched control, so it cannot distinguish energy-dependent attenuation from the benefit of reducing routed-update magnitudes more generally. A fixed coefficient near 0.96, leaving weight decay and non-routed updates unchanged, would provide an informative comparison, although it would not exactly match the update-norm budget. Appendix C.3 distinguishes these controls. Furthermore, we do not establish relative superiority over other expert-wise scaling methods, including Compass and Excitation, because native-method head-to-head comparisons were not performed.

Geometry and causal interpretation. The geometric analysis provides motivation for attenuation, not a causal explanation of loss spikes. The inverse-stable-rank identity describes the operator norm of MuonH’s trial update, not the final projected or stored parameter displacement, and does not directly apply to plain Muon. Moreover, the energy statistic depends on both spectral concentration and direction amplitude, rather than stable rank alone. In two examined events, single-update interventions substantially reduce the nominated parameter movements but fail to prevent the subsequent loss spikes. Thus, the full-schedule benefits cannot be explained simply as immediate removal of these two events through one-step attenuation. Effects accumulated over training, including changes in expert parameters or routing dynamics, remain possible explanations but are not established here. These negative interventions limit the mechanistic interpretation without negating the observed benefits of continuous calibration.

Scope, measurement, and generalizability. Both cohorts use one custom 4B-parameter, 128-expert, top-2 MoE model and 1.31B training tokens per run, with three initialization seeds and a shared data order. The results therefore do not establish generalization across architectures, scales, data distributions, or training budgets. Cohort H selects baselines within bounded learning-rate grids whose best-tested values lie at the lower boundaries; Cohort M fixes the plain-Muon recipe rather than independently retuning every variant. Reported standard deviations describe run-to-run variation, not confidence intervals. The adaptive spike detector can miss persistent loss elevation, while periodic validation may miss transient quality changes. Selected spectral measurements are not an all-layer census, and the local probes omit the subsequent router-bias-controller update.

EnergyCal applies a simple, one-sided attenuation to routed-expert updates using finite-step Newton–Schulz direction energy. In a 4B-parameter sparse MoE model, it substantially reduces thresholded loss-spike burden with both MuonH and plain Muon, showing that stabilization is also observed without Hyperball in the evaluated setting. The frozen EnergyCal–MuonH recipe reduces mean burden by 99.51% and final geometric-mean perplexity by 4.06% relative to a development-selected, lower-rate MuonH recipe, with 1.62% lower mean throughput. In a separate plain-Muon study at matched nominal learning rate and weight decay, reductions in mean burden average 95.98% across the two tested exponents, with small endpoint gains. These results support empirical stabilization in the evaluated MoE setting rather than general optimizer superiority. However, single-update interventions did not rescue two examined spikes, and the absence of a routed-only uniform-scaling control leaves the specific contribution of energy-dependent attenuation unresolved. Further controlled comparisons are needed to distinguish this contribution from reduced update magnitude.
